stop_loss_framework.method: volatility-scaled stop with constant dollar-risk position sizing
stop_loss_framework.stop_distance_rule: 2x the name's trailing average daily range ((high-low)/close), floored at 3%
stop_loss_framework.rationale: The user runs tight, large-quantum stops by design and will continue to (confirmed 2026-07-27); the stops are an emotional-tolerance control, not a technical signal. The prior failure mode was stop distance set without reference to a name's volatility -- a 3% stop on a name that ranges 8-9% intraday is a near-certain whipsaw. Constant-risk sizing resolves the apparent tension between 'wide stops' and 'small losses': a wider stop automatically produces a SMALLER position, so the dollar loss stays capped at 0.5% of book either way. DESIGN INTENT: worst case with every stop firing sits inside the -15% drawdown_warn rung, so the stop system can never by itself trigger the de-risking ladder. CORRECTED 2026-08-30 -- this file asserted that worst case was '~7.4% of book' as though it were a standing property. It is not; it is an OUTCOME of how much is deployed and at what volatility, and it drifts. Measured 11.947% on 2026-08-30 and 13.028% on 08-26, against the 10% aggregate_open_risk_cap_pct_of_book below -- i.e. the cap has been BREACHED, not merely approached. `smith_math.py validate` now fails on aggregate_over_cap so this can never again run for weeks as an unread line in a table. Any new position competes for a budget that is currently overdrawn and must be funded by reducing risk elsewhere.
stop_loss_framework.review_note: Daily-range inputs should be refreshed from a trailing 20-day window, not a single session; the 2026-07-27 seeding used Friday 07-24 ranges only.

support_anchored_exception.rule: For a REBOUND ENTRY only, and only when a real support level below spot is supplied and cited, size off the actual stop -- just under that support -- instead of 2xATR below spot. stop_distance_pct = max(distance_to_support, 0.5 x atr20_pct, 3.0).
support_anchored_exception.risk_is_unchanged: This does NOT loosen the risk budget. The same 0.5% of book is at risk if the stop fires; it is simply measured where the stop actually sits rather than at an arbitrary 2xATR. Verified: risk-at-cap is identical to the standard rule for every volatility tier.
support_anchored_exception.why_the_floor: A 4% stop on a 14%-ATR name is exactly the whipsaw this framework's main rationale was written to prevent. The support-anchored stop may be tighter than 2x the noise band because it rests on a real level, but never inside HALF a day's normal movement. The floor doubles as the uplift bound and is why no separate cap is needed: standard is 2xATR and the tightest permitted is 0.5xATR, so the exception can never size more than 4x the standard cap.
support_anchored_exception.aggregate_cap_still_binds: aggregate_open_risk_cap_pct_of_book applies unchanged. As of 2026-08-30 it is BREACHED (13.2% vs 10%), so a rebound entry must be FUNDED by reducing risk elsewhere -- typically the buy leg of a paired rotation -- not added on top. The sizing path stamps the funding shortfall on the proposal.
support_anchored_exception.rationale: Added 2026-08-30 on explicit user instruction, after modelling showed the standard rule structurally penalises exactly the names a rebound mandate wants. Constant-dollar-risk sizing makes max_position inversely proportional to ATR, so a 14%-ATR name gets ~1/7th the allowance of a 1.9%-ATR name and is flagged over-cap 38% of the time against 11% for low-vol names. That is correct for an entry with no view on where the name holds, and wrong for one bought AT a level. smith-rebound already computes support_usd; this makes the sizing consume it.

monthly_contribution_note: User commits USD 1,000 of NEW external cash per month starting 2026-08 (confirmed 2026-07-27). ~2.5% of current book per month. Deployment rule: direct each month's contribution to the cluster furthest BELOW its target_pct, and within that cluster to the lowest-volatility name with the most headroom under its constant-risk position cap. This is the structural antidote to the stop-out cycle -- fresh capital arrives every month regardless of whether stops fired, so redeployment never depends on conviction returning at a low.

normal.description: Steady-state operating band. Applies when no stop-loss event has fired in the prior 15 trading sessions.

post_stop_event.trigger: Any session in which stop-outs raise cash above 20% of total book. Regime persists for 15 trading sessions from the last stop-out, or until cash re-enters the normal band, whichever comes first.
post_stop_event.glide: Redeploy toward the normal band at whatever pace the volatility-scaled position caps permit (stop_loss_framework: 0.5% risk per position at 2x ATR20). Redeployment is NEVER forced by the calendar -- if the caps do not allow it, cash stays high and that is a correct outcome, not a breach.
post_stop_event.description: Elevated band that applies after a mass stop-out. Recognises that a tight, large-quantum stop discipline on a maximally-correlated book structurally converts equity to cash in single sessions.

cash_regimes.rationale: REVISED 2026-07-28 on explicit user instruction. The prior single [3,15]% band was an inherited default -- policy.json's own notes flagged it as not derived from this book's behaviour. It is incompatible with the user's confirmed stop-loss method, which has now twice liquidated a large fraction of the book in one session (2026-07-24: cash to 45.8%; 2026-07-28: cash to 60.5%). Under the old band, every post-stop-event day reported a severe breach the desk could not cure without violating the position-risk framework -- a false alarm that trained the reader to ignore a real control. The two-regime band separates 'cash is high because stops fired' (expected, tolerated to 40%) from 'cash is high because we are not deploying' (a genuine breach). Above 40% remains a real breach requiring action in either regime.
cash_regimes.current_note: As of 2026-07-28 cash is ~47.9% of book -- above even the post_stop_event ceiling of 40%, so this remains a live breach, not a tolerated level.

cluster_denominator_conditional.rule: While cash exceeds the NORMAL band top (15%), cluster CEILINGS are tested on TOTAL BOOK; cluster FLOORS are always tested on INVESTED EQUITY. Below that cash level both edges use invested equity.
cluster_denominator_conditional.rationale: User-raised 2026-07-28 and accepted. Rebuilding a book from a large cash position takes weeks, and cluster percentages computed on a shrunken equity base manufacture breaches that cannot be cured without violating the position-risk framework -- the third instance of the same denominator defect this week (Power floor binding at $29,870; cash band reporting an uncurable breach; now cluster ceilings). Cash is genuinely uncorrelated, so total book is the honest measure of factor risk while it is elevated. WHAT THIS DOES NOT DO: it does not relax per-position risk caps. A name at 1.6x its 0.5%-risk cap is oversized on either denominator -- SNDK on 2026-07-28 is the live example.
cluster_denominator_conditional.both_emitted: cmd_drift always emits actual_pct_of_equity and actual_pct_of_total_book regardless of basis tested.
cluster_denominator_conditional.why_split: A ceiling asks 'am I over-exposed to this factor?' -- idle cash is uncorrelated, so total book is the honest denominator. A floor asks 'is the invested portfolio the right shape?' -- that is a construction question, and 'hold 10% of TOTAL BOOK in Power' is incoherent while deliberately holding 48% cash. Testing both edges on one denominator was tried first and manufactured five phantom floor breaches.

cluster_playbooks_note: Added 2026-09-08 with cmd_ladder and smith-cluster. ONE agent definition is dispatched once per cluster; the cluster-specific knowledge -- the axes that actually decide which name wins inside THIS cluster -- lives here as DATA rather than in seven agent prompt files that would drift apart and each re-derive the shared output contract. Editable without touching a prompt. `slug` becomes the agent key (cluster_<slug>) and the slice/tail filename, so it must be unique and stable; changing one orphans that cluster's dispatch for a run. `differentiators` are the ranking axes the agent must actually rank on -- a ladder that re-states price is the thing this whole layer exists to replace. `read_throughs` are the cross-member inferences a per-name agent structurally cannot make.

differentiators: share of WFE spend captured, and whether that share is rising or defended
process-step mix -- litho vs deposition vs etch vs metrology vs test -- and which steps gain intensity as gate-all-around and advanced packaging ramp
leading-edge vs mature-node revenue split, and exposure to mature-node overcapacity
China export-control exposure: revenue at risk, licences held, and domestic substitution
foundry/IDM customer concentration and whether the customer is itself gaining share
advanced packaging (CoWoS-class) capacity as a distinct bottleneck from wafer capacity
read_throughs: TSMC monthly revenue -> the whole cluster's near-term utilisation
any WFE guide-down -> test (TER) usually lags the front end, do not assume synchrony

differentiators: HBM qualification status at each of NVDA / AMD / Broadcom, and at which HBM generation
HBM4 sampling timing and committed capacity vs announced capacity
DRAM vs NAND revenue mix, and the direction of each cycle independently
contract-price pass-through: how much of a spot move reaches this supplier's realised ASP
conventional-DRAM crowd-out -- HBM wafer conversion tightening commodity supply
enterprise SSD exposure as a separate AI-adjacent driver from DRAM
read_throughs: SK Hynix quarterly and guidance -> MU, and directionally -> SKHY itself
TrendForce contract guide -> the whole cluster's next-quarter ASP
a hyperscaler capex cut -> HBM before commodity DRAM

differentiators: 800G -> 1.6T transition timing, and who is qualified at 1.6T today vs promising it
co-packaged optics as a THREAT to pluggable-module economics -- who is disintermediated
position in the stack: laser/EML supply vs module assembly vs switch silicon vs connector
scale-up (within-rack) vs scale-out (between-rack) exposure -- different growth rates
custom-ASIC attach: whose silicon rides which hyperscaler's in-house accelerator
merchant switch silicon share vs in-house displacement risk
read_throughs: CIEN print -> LITE and COHR on component demand, with a lag
a hyperscaler naming an in-house NIC/switch -> merchant silicon exposure in this cluster
laser/EML lead times -> module makers' next-quarter gross margin, not revenue

differentiators: turbine and grid-equipment BACKLOG and its delivery window -- backlog is not revenue timing
liquid-cooling attach rate per rack, and whether it is priced as content or as a service
interconnection-queue and permitting exposure -- the real constraint on datacenter builds
behind-the-meter vs grid-connected power, and which regulatory regime each faces
fuel cell / on-site generation as a distinct bet from grid equipment
utility capex cycle exposure that is INDEPENDENT of AI datacenter demand
read_throughs: a hyperscaler datacenter announcement -> the local utility and the grid-equipment supplier
a large PPA or nuclear/gas offtake -> power names before cooling names
GEV/VRT order books -> the cluster's demand read; solar (FSLR) is policy-driven and should NOT be read as an AI-capex signal

differentiators: capex as a share of operating cash flow -- who is self-funding the build and who is not
in-house accelerator progress, which reduces merchant silicon spend but raises own capex
cloud revenue growth vs capex growth -- the gap is the market's real question
neocloud financing structure: debt, GPU collateral, and contracted vs speculative capacity
customer contract duration and counterparty quality for the neoclouds specifically
depreciation-schedule changes as an earnings-quality tell
read_throughs: any hyperscaler capex guide -> the entire AI-capex book, this is the apex read-through
a neocloud financing round or GPU-backed facility -> the whole neocloud sub-group's cost of capital, not just the issuer

differentiators: gross margin per rack and whether it is holding as volume scales -- the core OEM question
direct-to-hyperscaler vs channel mix
liquid-cooling rack integration capability as a differentiator vs a commodity
working capital and inventory turns -- an OEM's real risk is a balance sheet, not demand
governance, audit and filing history (a live, name-specific issue in this cluster)
read_throughs: an NVDA allocation shift -> OEM revenue timing before OEM margin
any rack-scale reference-design change -> the integrator's requalification cost

differentiators: automotive vs industrial vs personal-electronics end-market mix and each cycle's phase
inventory correction stage at distributors -- the dominant driver in this cluster
internal vs foundry manufacturing and the fixed-cost drag at low utilisation
pricing discipline as prior-cycle price increases unwind
this cluster is a NON-AI-capex diversifier -- rank it on its own cycle, and say so explicitly if the ranking is being contaminated by AI-capex read-across
read_throughs: any analog peer's inventory commentary -> the whole cluster's correction stage
